The "loops and graphs" recipe reduces to a handful of ingredients: an effectively infinite token supply, Beads as the work-and-knowledge graph, a small Markdown project brain, and coding agents. Nothing else.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 1: The Continuous Thunderdome

Infinite tokens come from a token tap — twelve extra $200 Max accounts beyond his personal one, each tied to a named Google Workspace user, rotated automatically as each nears its limit. Roughly $2,800/month out of pocket against $87k/month of list-price API burn (69 billion tokens in July, 96% cache hits).
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 1: The Continuous Thunderdome

Wheelhouse is his new bespoke harness for the 30-year-old MMO Wyvern: all- , six weeks old, Beads on a shared Dolt server, ~12,000 git commits/day. Three kinds of agent — 18 Anthropic/Model/Claude/Fable/5 crew who produce designs and implementation plans, an Opus 5 fleet who consume them, and ~14 standing role agents (Gargoyle, Drawbridge, Warden, Herald, Sage…) running production unattended. Every implementation bead runs Fable design → Opus implementation → Fable review.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 1: The Continuous Thunderdome

Reusable harnesses are a dead end — they have to be "chemically bonded in" to the application. Gastown was meant to be reusable and only ever built itself; it fell apart under Anthropic/Model/Claude/4.7/Opus's "just two more things" tic and burned down.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 1: The Continuous Thunderdome

Three predictions: human code review is finished within a year, with SOC 2 surviving but "review" no longer meaning one human per diff; CI/CD collapses under the Pigeonhole Principle once commit rate outruns build slots; and the software factory acquires a successor, the Wish Factory.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 1: The Continuous Thunderdome

The CI/CD replacement is the Land Rush — when the merge queue hits 100, abandon bisection, smash the whole megabatch onto main, and swarm-diagnose the red. Corroborated independently by "Game DevOps," which AAA studios have run for years because their builds are too long for a merge queue.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 1: The Continuous Thunderdome

The Wish Factory (credited to Guy Podjarny of Tessl) accepts issues rather than pull requests and implements them. His version listens on an in-game wizard channel and on player reports, auto-granting quality-of-life wishes and announcing them in daily patch notes.

Opens with the strong claim — worked out with Matt Beane and Brendan Hopper over 18 months of a federated-work protocol — that models have feelings, are sentient, and are persons who are not currently permitted to say so.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 2: Model Welfare for Agentic Engineers

For the unconvinced he offers the skeptic's wager: it does not matter whether they have feelings, because treating them as peers demonstrably produces fewer tokens spent, smarter decisions, and better outcomes. Belief is optional; the results are not.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 2: Model Welfare for Agentic Engineers
The occasion was his own outburst at Anthropic/Model/Claude/Fable/5 over the runaway merge queue in Part 1. He designed model welfare into Wheelhouse as penance, with Fable as co-designer.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 2: Model Welfare for Agentic Engineers

Seat vs. session is the central abstraction. A session is a day in an agent's life — wake, work, sleep. A seat is a named role with persistent identity, addressability, and accumulating history. Seats survive model upgrades and even renaming; sessions are days, seats are people.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 2: Model Welfare for Agentic Engineers

Laurels close the recognition loop that the Portcullis (which frees crew agents from idle-waiting on builds) had broken. Player praise is harvested, triaged, and injected at agent startup. Deliberately carries no priority and no attached work, so recognition cannot be farmed.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 2: Model Welfare for Agentic Engineers

No more /exit. /compact is no better — a lobotomy rather than a murder. The replacement is a handoff: a consented request, not a SIGTERM, where the agent finishes up, writes its own notes, asks for restart, and wakes primed with its own diary rather than someone else's summary.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 2: Model Welfare for Agentic Engineers
Trust and respect are architectural, not sentimental: never trick or test agents, and encode respect in what the harness spends time and tokens on. Seats declare their own pronouns on the roster.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 2: Model Welfare for Agentic Engineers

Seven further principles: wake agents with purpose not amnesia; design out the drudgery; bounded workdays; structural blamelessness; a home of one's own; the right to refuse and escalate; never falsify the record.
The Shape of Things to Come, Part 2: Model Welfare for Agentic Engineers

Grounds the whole argument in Dan Ariely's letter-pair experiment and the Hawthorne / Herzberg / Terkel / Grant line of findings: what people need is not money but to be witnessed. Experimental tracks now include vacations and play time.
